precepts.text: Zerubbabel's wisdom before the king shows that a woman holds power over even the great king, so Esther should not fear to use the influence she has.
precepts.point: So Mordecai went his way and did according to all Esther commanded him. She had her mind set right, ready to risk her life for her people.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

precepts.why:
Esther sets her mind: “so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.” She is ready to risk her life for her people. But she is not going in with nothing; she is a woman, and a woman holds power over even the great king.

Zerubbabel proved that before the king in his wisdom: “is not the king great in his power? do not all regions fear to touch him? Yet did I see him and Apame the king’s concubine, the daughter of the admirable Bartacus, sitting at the right hand of the king, And taking the crown from the king’s head, and setting it upon her own head; she also struck the king with her left hand. And yet for all this the king gaped and gazed upon her with open mouth: if she laughed upon him, he laughed also: but if she took any displeasure at him, the king was fain to flatter, that she might be reconciled to him again.”

All regions feared to touch the king, and a woman took the crown off his head and struck him, and he flattered her to be reconciled. So Esther should not fear to use the influence she has. The law said death for coming in uncalled, but a woman's influence over the king was real, and she went in to use it for Israel.

precepts.text: The things written beforetime were written for our learning, which is why Mordecai would not accept a weak answer from Esther but held her to her purpose.
precepts.point: So Mordecai went his way and did according to all Esther commanded him. She had her mind set right, ready to risk her life for her people.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

precepts.why:
“So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.” He would not accept a weak answer from her; he held her to her purpose until she answered, “if I perish, I perish.”

“For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.” This is why the account is written: for our learning. Esther with her mind set right, ready to risk her life for her people, and Mordecai holding her to it, are written so that we, through patience and the comfort of the scriptures, might have hope.

precepts.text: Mardocheus rent his clothes, put on sackcloth with ashes, went out into the city, and cried with a loud and bitter cry.
precepts.point: All Israel in like manner cried most earnestly unto the Lord because their death was before their eyes. Mardocheus rent his clothes and cried through the city with a loud and bitter cry, as the canonical account records.

note.label: Esther 13: The Decree of Destruction and the Prayer of Mardocheus

precepts.why:
The prayer of Mardocheus is what he prayed; the canonical book shows what he did. “When Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and a bitter cry”. The man who would not bow to proud Aman, and who told the Lord it “was neither in contempt nor pride, nor for any desire of glory”, went out into the midst of the city in sackcloth and ashes, crying aloud.

That loud and bitter cry is the “Hear my prayer” of the Apocrypha: “spare thy people: for their eyes are upon us to bring us to nought”. Their death was before their eyes, and Mardocheus cried it through the city as he cried it to the Most High.

precepts.text: In every province where the king's decree came there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and wailing, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
precepts.point: All Israel in like manner cried most earnestly unto the Lord because their death was before their eyes. Mardocheus rent his clothes and cried through the city with a loud and bitter cry, as the canonical account records.

note.label: Esther 13: The Decree of Destruction and the Prayer of Mardocheus

precepts.why:
“All Israel in like manner cried most earnestly unto the Lord, because their death was before their eyes.” The canonical book records it province by province: “in every province, whithersoever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.”

It was not Mardocheus alone. Wherever the decree came, the whole nation mourned, fasted, wept and wailed, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes as he did. That is “All Israel in like manner”: a nation with death before its eyes crying most earnestly to the Most High to spare his people and turn their sorrow into joy.

precepts.text: Whosoever came to the king into the inner court uncalled would be put to death, except the king held out the golden sceptre.
precepts.point: Then God changed the spirit of the king into mildness. He leaped from his throne, took her in his arms until she came to herself, and comforted her with loving words. The Most High turned the king's heart.
precepts.why:
Her “countenance was cheerful and very amiable: but her heart was in anguish for fear”, and the fear had a reason. Esther herself had said it: “whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.”

The only time anyone could come before the king was when called, and she had not been called in thirty days. She was coming without going through the proper order, with one law standing against her. So when the king, “very dreadful” in his robes of majesty, “looked very fiercely upon her”, the queen “fell down, and was pale, and fainted”. She was looking at the law of death, with only the golden sceptre between her and it.

points: Mordecai put her in her place: she was in the king's house to go to the king for her people, and holding her peace would not shield her there.
If you pull back, the deliverance comes from another place. He does not need you, but you do not want to be the one cast aside.
Who knows whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this. Nobody here was woken up at this time by chance.

When Mordecai perceived all that was done he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth with ashes, went out into the midst of the city and cried with a loud and bitter cry, and came before the king's gate, for none might enter it clothed with sackcloth.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: In every province where the king's commandment and decree came there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping and wailing, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes. Imagine a decree today to kill every descendant of Israel, and you begin to feel what they went through.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: Esther's maids and chamberlain told her, and the queen was exceedingly grieved and sent raiment to clothe Mordecai and take away his sackcloth, but he received it not. She sent Hatach, appointed to attend her, to learn what it was and why.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: Mordecai told Hatach all that had happened and of the money Haman promised to pay for the Jews to be destroyed, and gave him a copy of the decree published in Shushan to show Esther, charging her to go in to the king and make supplication for her people.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: Esther answered by Hatach that all the king's servants and people knew that whosoever came unto the king in the inner court uncalled, man or woman, there was one law, to be put to death, except the king held out the golden sceptre that he may live.

She said she had not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days, and they told Mordecai her words. She made an excuse, though she was the queen the king had chosen and loved above all the women.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: Mordecai sent answer that Esther should not think she would escape in the king's house more than all the Jews, for if she altogether held her peace at this time, then enlargement and deliverance would arise to the Jews from another place, but she and her father's house would be destroyed.

Who knoweth whether Esther was come to the kingdom for such a time as this. She was put in her position to serve this very purpose, and the deliverance of Israel cannot be held back; she would either help it along or be left behind while it came another way.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: Esther returned answer that Mordecai should gather all the Jews in Shushan to fast for her, neither eating nor drinking three days, night or day, and she and her maidens would fast likewise, and so she would go in unto the king not according to the law, and if she perished, she perished.

note.label: Esther 4: Mordecai Charges Esther for Such a Time as This

points: So Mordecai went his way and did according to all Esther commanded him. She had her mind set right, ready to risk her life for her people.
